title: Intestinal phase influences down-regulate gastric acid secretion after a meal
vignette: Experimental gastric function monitoring in healthy subjects before, during and after a meal shows an initial rise, peak, and then decline in gastric acid production. Which of the following helps most to down-regulate gastric secretion after a meal?

clues.text: initial rise, peak, and then decline in gastric acid production
clues.note: Acid secretion rises through the cephalic and gastric phases, then DECLINES as inhibitory intestinal-phase signals take over.

clues.text: down-regulate gastric secretion after a meal
clues.note: The intestinal phase supplies the main INHIBITORY signals: peptide YY, somatostatin, and prostaglandins that suppress gastrin-driven acid secretion.

whatMatters: After a meal, the INTESTINAL PHASE provides the dominant inhibitory signals: as chyme enters the duodenum, the ileum and colon release PEPTIDE YY (plus somatostatin and prostaglandins) that inhibit gastrin-stimulated histamine release from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells, down-regulating acid secretion. Answer D.
strategy: Split the three phases into stimulatory vs inhibitory. Cephalic (vagal) and gastric (gastrin, distension) phases STIMULATE acid; the INTESTINAL phase (peptide YY, somatostatin, prostaglandins, secretin) INHIBITS it once food reaches the duodenum. Reject basal secretion (baseline, not a down-regulator), cephalic phase and gastrin (stimulate), receptive relaxation (fundic accommodation reflex), and postprandial alkaline tide (a consequence of acid secretion, not a regulator).

eliminations.label: Basal secretion - baseline, not a down-regulator
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the low-level acid secreted in the absence of stimuli. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is the resting baseline, not a mechanism that suppresses postprandial secretion. ✅ Correct if: defining unstimulated (basal) acid output.

eliminations.label: Cephalic phase - stimulates acid
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: vagally mediated acid secretion triggered by the thought/sight/smell/taste of food. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it INCREASES acid secretion, the opposite of down-regulation. ✅ Correct if: what initiates acid secretion before food arrives.

eliminations.label: Gastrin release - stimulates acid
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: gastrin from G cells stimulating ECL cells (histamine) and parietal cells. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: gastrin is a major STIMULATOR of acid, not an inhibitor. ✅ Correct if: gastric-phase stimulation of secretion.

eliminations.label: Receptive relaxation - fundic accommodation
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a vagovagal reflex relaxing the gastric fundus to accommodate food. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it governs gastric volume/accommodation, not acid down-regulation. ✅ Correct if: fundic relaxation with swallowing.

eliminations.label: Postprandial alkaline tide - a consequence, not a regulator
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the rise in plasma bicarbonate (and fall in chloride) as parietal cells secrete H+ and add HCO3- to blood. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is a downstream CONSEQUENCE of acid secretion, not a factor that down-regulates it. ✅ Correct if: explaining the postmeal rise in venous bicarbonate.

reasoning: Acid secretion rises (cephalic + gastric phases) then declines after a meal
The decline is driven by inhibitory signals from the intestine
As chyme enters the duodenum, peptide YY / somatostatin / prostaglandins suppress gastrin-driven acid
-> intestinal influences down-regulate secretion; answer D
mechanism: Gastric acid secretion is classically divided into three phases. The CEPHALIC phase (vagal/cholinergic, triggered by thought, sight, smell, taste of food) and the GASTRIC phase (gastrin release and stomach distension, which drives histamine release from ECL cells and acid from parietal cells) are STIMULATORY, producing the postprandial rise and peak. The INTESTINAL phase then predominates in DOWN-REGULATING secretion: as protein-containing chyme enters the duodenum, the ileum and colon release PEPTIDE YY, which acts on ECL cells to counteract the cephalic/gastric drive by inhibiting gastrin-stimulated histamine release; SOMATOSTATIN and PROSTAGLANDINS provide additional inhibition (and duodenal acid triggers secretin). These signals cause the observed decline. Basal secretion is merely the unstimulated baseline; receptive relaxation is a motility reflex; and the postprandial alkaline tide is a metabolic consequence of acid secretion, not a regulator of it.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid GI > gastric acid phases: cephalic (vagal) + gastric (gastrin/distension) stimulate; intestinal phase inhibits (peptide YY, somatostatin, prostaglandins, secretin); ECL cells release histamine under gastrin control.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: The postmeal decline in acid is driven by inhibitory intestinal-phase signals (peptide YY).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on cephalic/gastric/intestinal phases, peptide YY, ECL cells, somatostatin, or alkaline tide? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Cephalic phase and gastrin STIMULATE; basal = baseline; receptive relaxation = motility; alkaline tide = consequence.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: intestinal phase (peptide YY/somatostatin/prostaglandins) down-regulates gastric acid after a meal.

memoryHook: The stomach revs up for the meal (cephalic + gastric), then the intestines tap the brakes - peptide YY tells the acid to stand down.
